extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism (especially readers of Northrop Frye), graduate literature students, and teachers of genre/theory
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Northrop Frye's Anatomy-of-Criticism schema to identify and classify literary works by mythos, character types, and phase; using imagery, plot, character, mood, and analogies as diagnostic criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of the four mythoi (comedy, romance, tragedy, irony) and their archetypal themes
rubrics_metrics.description: The four mythoi—comedy, romance, tragedy, and irony—are aspects of a central unifying myth; each has an archetypal theme (e.g., comedy: anagnorisis/recognition; romance: agon/conflict/sequence of marvelous adventures; tragedy: pathos/catastrophe; irony/satire: sparagmos/disorganization and foredoomed action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the archetypal theme as the defining feature when classifying a work's mythos. Example labels from the text: 'Agon or conflict is the basis or archetypal theme of romance,' 'Pathos or catastrophe ... is the archetypal theme of tragedy,' 'Sparagmos ... is the archetypal theme of irony and satire,' 'Anagnorisis ... is the archetypal theme of comedy.' These thematic identifications can be employed even when a work mixes features of more than one mythos, since Frye treats them as related poles of a unifying schema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure-as-theme: isolate the defining narrative movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of a mythos' structure depends on isolating one part of its narrative movement (e.g., in comedy it is the discovery/anagnorisis; in romance the conflict/quest). Frye treats 'theme' and 'narrative' as closely related: narrative may be seen as theme, and theme as a simultaneous unity in the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a work, identify the single narrative movement that functions as the structural core (discovery, quest/conflict, catastrophe, disorganization). This helps map the work onto the corresponding mythos even if other elements are present. Note Frye's use of Aristotle's anagnorisis to explain moments when perspective changes and a unifying structure is revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectical oppositions as primary methodological principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye builds categories via a series of opposing yet related pairs (e.g., alazon vs eiron; bomolochos vs agroikos; the innocence-experience vertical dialectic). Structure and mood form a general opposition that underlies character distribution and other distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify elements (character, plot, mood) in terms of binary or bipolar oppositions: determine which pole an element belongs to and map positions dialectically. Expect a double bipolar distribution of character types and phase-relations across the innocence/experience and realistic/ideal planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization by function: four stock types and their subtypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are stock types whose identity is determined by dramatic function rather than mere surface traits. Frye adapts Greek labels into four general categories: alazon (impostor/blocker), eiron (self-deprecator/trickster/hero), bomolochos (buffoon/clown), and agroikos (rustic/churl). Each category contains multiple subtypes and variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characters by the roles they play in the plot and mood (who blocks, who effects recognition, who produces festivity, who refuses festivity). Use extensive examples (senex iratus, miles gloriosus, trickster slaves, Figaro, Puck, Sancho Panza, Golux figures like nymphs or giants) to situate particular characters in Frye's schema rather than relying on surface realism. Recognize that the same character can have mixed or variant functions (e.g., an eiron who partly functions as an alazon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analogical methods (seasonal, ritual/dream, musical) to define mythoi
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye frequently defines mythoi via analogies—comparing literary action to seasonal cycles (comedy:spring; romance:summer), ritual and dream structures (removal of neurosis, search of libido), and musical form (spatial/temporal axes and schematic order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate analogies (seasonal cycles, ritual motifs, dream-psychology, musical form) to situate a work within Frye's mythic map; analogies move the frame outward and help identify general mythic behavior rather than particular plot events. Remember these analogies explain the typical mood and imagery of a mythos but do not substitute for close attention to plot and character function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase theory: six phases per mythos and phase identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Each pregeneric mythos consists of six distinguishable phases (phases 1–6). A 'phase' is a degree of variation from the norm and can be distinguished by criteria such as plot pattern, plot ending, character, imagery, mood, and audience perspective. Phases may be linear or cyclical depending on the mythos (e.g., romance is overtly cyclical; comedy has a linear arc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying a work's phase, examine which of the six positions it occupies by asking: Where in the sequence toward or away from the redeemed/ideal society does it lie? Use concrete markers (birth/infancy, adolescence, coming-of-age/quest, green-world/maturity, Arcadian/reflective distance, Gothic/penseroso collapse) with textual examples (e.g., Phase I: ironic/ birth-of-hero; Phase IV: green-world; Phase V: Arcadian reflective distance; Phase VI: Gothic/penseroso). Determine whether the work's movement is cyclical (hero's life in romance) or linear (comic total runs its course).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for differentiating phases: imagery, plot, character, mood, audience perspective, social unit size, hero's life-stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye differentiates phases by appealing to a set of principles—imagery (e.g., green/golden colors), theme, plot and its parts, character types and age, mood/tone (festive, pensive, occult), the perspective of the audience (e.g., fifth-phase detachment), and the size of the social unit (e.g., sixth-phase esoteric/small units).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a combination of these criteria rather than relying on any single marker. For example, distinguish fourth-phase romance by the visible 'happier society', the theme of maintaining innocent world, and particular images (beleaguered castle, monster tamed by virgin). For fifth-phase, weigh audience distance and reflective tone. For second-phase, look for youth/Arcadian pastoral imagery. Always triangulate with plot and character function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel relations among phases of adjacent mythoi
rubrics_metrics.description: Phases of one mythos correspond to phases of adjacent mythoi (e.g., phases 1–3 of comedy parallel 1–3 of irony; phases 4–6 of comedy parallel 4–6 of romance). Correspondences are established where specific characteristics (imagery, mood, social visibility, life-stage) line up across mythoi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing cross-genre affinities, map phases between mythoi by looking for shared dominant criteria. Example: fourth-phase comedy and romance both make the 'happier society' visible throughout; fifth-phase pairings emphasize natural cycles and detached, idyllic perspective; sixth-phase pairings show small/occult social units and contemplative withdrawal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition-by-illustration: extensive exemplification as a method
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye frequently defines types and phases by calling on a vast range of literary examples (e.g., eighty references in a twenty-two-page treatment). He uses illustration to specify subtypes and border cases rather than relying solely on strict definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In applying Frye's method, compile multiple canonical and marginal examples to substantiate category placement. Expect many borderline or mixed cases; use examples to show functional affinities (e.g., Fielding's Squire Airworthy as having the dramatic function of a senex without its characteristics). Avoid overreliance on single encyclopedic definitions—prefer comparative exemplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function over lifelikeness: stock types are compatible with lifelike characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Stock types ('skeletons') are necessary to dramatic function, but they do not imply caricature or lack of lifelikeness; lifelike characters 'owe their consistency to the appropriateness of the stock type which belongs to their dramatic function.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging characterization, prioritize function in the narrative structure; recognize that realistic depth coexists with archetypal function. Do not mistake stock-type labeling for a claim that the character is unconvincing—rather, it is the organising principle of their dramatic role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclic vs linear models: determine temporal/topical organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye emphasizes that some mythoi exhibit cyclical patterns (romance: hero's life cycles) while others show a more linear sequence (comic mythos runs its course and dies). The same category (phase) may be used differently depending on whether the model is cyclical or linear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work's pattern is best read as part of a recurring cycle (e.g., recurring heroic exploits, seasonal analogies) or as a one-way progression toward an end-state. This affects how phases are interpreted (a 'phase' in a cyclical mythos may be a repeating stage in a hero's life; in a linear mythos it marks movement toward termination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of audience perspective and rhetorical conventions as classificatory devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspective of the audience (e.g., feeling raised above action in fifth-phase comedy) and rhetorical devices (e.g., symposium device) serve as legitimate criteria for defining phases and distinguishing works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include metapoetic and rhetorical features—how a work positions its reader/viewer, devices of distancing or nesting (play-within-a-play)—in phase and mythos classification. These features can be decisive, especially in the middle-to-late phases where audience stance and rhetorical mode shape the mode's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-criterion diagnosis: combine narrow and broad principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye's definitions often combine very particular markers (imagery, age of hero, a single motif) with broad principles (vision of society, innocence/experience axis). A proper diagnosis mixes both narrow and wide-ranging criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce classification to a single sign. For strongest analytic claims, cite a constellation of criteria—imagery, plot movement, character function, mood, social vision—to show how they converge on a particular mythos/phase assignment. Recognize that some correspondences are 'tenuous, but not quite a distinction without a difference.'
